lead: An electrode potential is not a fixed number. Change the ion concentration around an electrode and its potential moves. The Nernst equation gives that shift, linking measured EMF to the reaction quotient Q. Read through ΔG = −nFE, the same equation ties cell voltage to Gibbs free energy and to the equilibrium constant K. Engineers use it to see how a battery's voltage sags as it drains, and to turn a measured voltage into a concentration. Only a few universities teach the full thermodynamic depth; the working equations below are what exams ask.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for cell EMF and single electrode potentials, and Unit 3 for Gibbs free energy and the equilibrium constant.

blocks.text: A cell gives EMF because its reaction is not at equilibrium. As products build up, the driving force falls. The Nernst equation puts that fall into numbers, using Q, the reaction quotient: products over reactants, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient.

blocks.where: E is the cell EMF in volts; E° is the standard EMF in volts, measured with every species at unit activity (1 M for solutes, 1 bar for gases); R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the gas constant; T is temperature in kelvin; n is the number of electrons in the balanced cell reaction; F = 96485 C mol⁻¹ is the Faraday constant, the charge on one mole of electrons; Q is the reaction quotient.

blocks.text: At 298 K the constants collapse into one number: RT/F = 8.314 × 298 ÷ 96485 = 0.0257 V, and ln x = 2.303 log₁₀ x, which gives 0.0592 V.

blocks.where: valid only at 298 K; 0.0592 has units of volts; the log is base 10.

items: Metal/metal-ion: for Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ → M, Q = 1/[Mⁿ⁺], so E = E° + (0.0592/n) log[Mⁿ⁺]. The potential rises with ion concentration.
Gas electrode: for 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, Q = p(H₂)/[H⁺]², so E = E° − (0.0592/2) log(p(H₂)/[H⁺]²).
Redox electrode: for Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺, Q = [Fe²⁺]/[Fe³⁺], so E = E° − 0.0592 log([Fe²⁺]/[Fe³⁺]).

blocks.text: A cell that delivers charge does electrical work. Sending n faradays through a potential difference of E volts delivers nFE joules, and at constant temperature and pressure that work comes out of the Gibbs free energy.

blocks.where: ΔG is the Gibbs free energy change of the cell reaction in J mol⁻¹; n is electrons transferred; F = 96485 C mol⁻¹; E is the cell EMF in volts, and 1 C × 1 V = 1 J.

blocks.text: The sign carries the meaning. A positive E gives a negative ΔG, so the reaction runs and the cell works. A dead battery has E = 0 and Q = K.

blocks.where: ΔG° is the standard free energy change in J mol⁻¹, E° the standard EMF in volts, K the equilibrium constant of the cell reaction.

blocks.text: E° = (RT/nF) ln K = (0.0592/n) log₁₀ K at 298 K
blocks.where: a large positive E° means K ≫ 1; at n = 1, every 0.0592 V is a tenfold change in K.

blocks.text: Temperature coefficient. Because ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, measuring E at several temperatures separates the two: ΔS = nF(∂E/∂T) and ΔH = −nFE + nFT(∂E/∂T), at constant pressure. An EMF that falls as temperature rises means a negative ΔS.

figure.caption: Cell EMF falls in a straight line as log Q rises, for n = 2 and E° = 1.10 V. The slope is −0.0592/n = −0.0296 V per decade, so a tenfold rise in Q costs 29.6 mV.

spec.aria: A straight line falls as log Q increases, showing the Nernst equation for a two-electron cell with E° equal to 1.10 V.

examples.question: For the cell Zn | Zn²⁺(0.10 M) || Cu²⁺(1.0 M) | Cu at 298 K, E° = 1.10 V and F = 96485 C mol⁻¹. Write the cell reaction, calculate the cell EMF, and calculate ΔG in kJ mol⁻¹.
steps: Cell reaction: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. Zinc is oxidised, copper ion is reduced, and n = 2 electrons.
Reaction quotient: Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] = 0.10/1.0 = 0.10. The solids Zn and Cu have activity 1 and do not appear.
Free energy: ΔG = −nFE = −2 × 96485 × 1.1296 = −217979 J mol⁻¹ = −218 kJ mol⁻¹.
Check the sign: ΔG is negative and E is above E°, both consistent with Q < 1.
examples.answer: E = 1.1296 V (about 1.13 V) and ΔG = −218 kJ mol⁻¹, so the cell reaction is spontaneous as written.
examples.check:
import math
E0 = 1.10
n = 2
F = 96485
Zn = 0.10
Cu = 1.0
Q = Zn / Cu
logQ = math.log10(Q)
E = E0 - (0.0592 / n) * logQ
G = -n * F * E / 1000
print(round(E, 4))
print(round(G, 1))

traps: 0.0592 V goes with log base 10. Using it beside ln inflates the answer by 2.303.
Q is products over reactants, and pure solids and liquids have activity 1, so Zn and Cu metal never appear in Q.
n is the number of electrons in the balanced cell reaction, not the charge on one ion; for Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, n = 2.
ΔG = −nFE gives joules per mole. Divide by 1000 before writing kJ mol⁻¹.
Keep the minus sign in E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q. If Q < 1, log Q is negative and E lies above E°.

quiz.q: Write the Nernst equation for a cell at 298 K and name every symbol.
quiz.a: E = E° − (0.0592/n) log₁₀ Q. E and E° are cell EMF and standard EMF in volts, n is the electrons transferred in the balanced reaction, Q is the reaction quotient.

quiz.q: Why does a Cu²⁺/Cu electrode potential rise when [Cu²⁺] rises?
quiz.a: For Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, Q = 1/[Cu²⁺], so E = E° + (0.0296) log[Cu²⁺]. More Cu²⁺ pushes reduction forward and the potential rises.

quiz.q: A one-electron cell has E° = 0.80 V. Find E at 298 K when Q = 1 × 10⁻³.
A two-electron cell has E° = 0.46 V at 298 K. Find K.
A Daniell cell discharges. How do Q, E and ΔG move, and where do they stop?
quiz.a: Zn²⁺ rises and Cu²⁺ falls, so Q rises; E falls and ΔG = −nFE becomes less negative. At equilibrium Q = K, E = 0, ΔG = 0.

quiz.q: Two cells share the same E° but have n = 1 and n = 2. Which E drops more when Q rises tenfold, and by how much?
quiz.a: The n = 1 cell, by 0.0592 V. The n = 2 cell drops by 0.0296 V, because the slope is −0.0592/n.

quiz.q: Why does a large positive E° mean the reaction goes almost to completion?
quiz.a: E° = (0.0592/n) log K, so a large E° means a large K, and products dominate at equilibrium.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real electrolytes are not ideal, so careful work replaces concentration with activity. Plotting E against pH and potential gives a Pourbaix diagram, which maps the stable form of a metal in water. pH meters and ion-selective electrodes invert the Nernst equation to read concentration from a voltage (see 4.4). Search next for activity coefficient, Pourbaix diagram and liquid junction potential.
